« Face à l’injustice et lorsqu’on a mal,: “When faced with injustice and when you’re hurting, you need to step back for a moment”
Les intervenants invités du CARI Saint-L: Guest community workers from CARI Saint-Laurent, Mélissa Jean-Baptiste and Faty Diambang, with participants accompanied by Horiol Destinée and Wideline Joseph of the organization ICI Montréal-Nord.
À Montréal comme ailleurs, le racisme qu: In Montréal as elsewhere, the racism that Black people face creeps into certain institutions and shows up in the most mundane everyday interactions. Black people in the city have to contend with this reality regardless of their immigration status, their country of origin or their social class. At the suggestion of Horiol Desile Destiné, project manager at ICI Montréal-Nord, La Converse welcomed about twenty people to discuss, in particular, the issues and solutions related to anti-Black racism in Montréal. Although complementary, the views diverge, between a interventionist position grounded in the law and an approach concerned with taking into account, among other things, the stress and psychological consequences of such steps.
Parmi les invités, des intervenants en i: Among the guests were social integration workers such as Faty Diambang and Mélissa Jean-Baptiste, who work for CARI Saint-Laurent, an organization specializing in the integration of newcomers. Residents were also invited to share their experiences and opinions on the subject. Horiol Desile Destiné, who works on the Échec au racisme project at ICI Montréal-Nord (Intégration, citoyenneté et inclusion), is accompanied by Wideline Joseph, who works at the same organization. Once everyone has arrived, the dialogue begins.
Cette initiative s’inscrit dans le cadre: The initiative is part of the International Decade for People of African Descent, Horiol explains. Wanting to have a frank discussion to equip Black people who have recently settled in Montréal, the organization is taking part in the dialogue with the community workers introduced above and a group of newcomers. Settled comfortably among cushions or in the ergonomic chairs of our office, some with notebook and pen in hand, the participants introduce themselves one by one, ready to dive into the discussion.
D’emblée, lorsqu’on demande à Faty Diamb: Right off the bat, when Faty Diambang and Mélissa Jean-Baptiste of CARI Saint-Laurent are asked what their days look like, they describe their experiences as immigration counsellors working with newcomers and asylum seekers. Mélissa, who supports them day to day, stresses how prolonged waits for work permits are a source of financial stress for asylum seekers. “Immigration says it normally takes three months, but some have been waiting for a year. It’s long; some are waiting on hearing delays to find out whether their status will be accepted. It takes time, there are people who wait three years, four years,” she says.
Trouver un logement à prix abordable est: Finding affordable housing is also a challenge, particularly in the current context. “Finding a 4½ or a 5½ for $1,200 is very rare – as much for me as for them or for the average person,” she says. Mélissa also supports asylum seekers no matter what they need: using a food bank, getting clothing, signing up for French classes, going back to school, finding a new job, and so on. She says this happens mostly in cases of workplace abuse, when a person is mistreated or someone refuses to pay them. Her colleague Faty adds that asylum seekers face precarity, and a power imbalance that works against them and crushes them, even when they have someone at their side. “We often feel powerless in the face of what they bring us, it’s a really heavy machine,” he says with regret.
Plusieurs participants lèvent à leur tou: Several participants raise their hands in turn to share what they have experienced since arriving in Montréal. One of them, a young man from Haiti, says he has been turned down repeatedly after applying for jobs. Yet “all those job interviews had gone very well,” he says. Despite the studies he completed in his home country, his ability to express himself in French and his enthusiasm, nothing works; no one calls him back. For him, there is no doubt: “It’s clearly because of the colour of my skin that I’m going through this string of misfortunes.” Around him, people shake and nod their heads in disapproval or to show they are not surprised.
Outre le soutien qu’il apporte aux immig: Besides the support it provides to recent immigrants and asylum seekers, CARI also gives technical help to permanent residents and long-time immigrants with their immigration applications. Integration counsellors also offer support in searching for housing and jobs and can refer users to outside resources when needed.
Mais que faire lorsqu’une simple formali: But what can be done when a simple formality becomes an obstacle to human dignity? Mélissa recounts the recent case of a person who experienced racism in a medical setting. Thanks to training offered by the Clinique juridique de Saint-Michel, she and her colleagues were able to refer the complainant, in an informed way, to legal aid services. These are available at little cost to low-income people, as is often the case for newcomers.
En cas de traitement discriminatoire au: In cases of discriminatory treatment when receiving care, “no matter your status, even if it’s precarious, you have the right to a second medical opinion, you have the right to tell the doctor: ‘I’m not sure about what you’re telling me and I think you’re treating me unfairly,’ ”, the community worker says. “People tend to think that if I speak up, [the Canadian authorities] won’t give me permanent residence; if I speak up, the judge will send me back to my country and my application will be rejected. There’s that fear.”
Wideline Joseph, organisatrice communaut: Wideline Joseph, community organizer at ICI Montréal-Nord, believes this fear weighs heavily. She also raises another point: how racialized newcomers perceive the services offered here. Indeed, in their countries of origin, some are used to experiencing discriminatory treatment based on their social class or colourism (discrimination based on darker or lighter skin pigmentation). So, according to Wideline, “suffering negative things that call their dignity into question is normal, because not only do they not have legal status, they also have a precarious financial status.”
Selon elle, « l’aspect culturel des gens: In her view, “the cultural background of the people we work with is important.” “We have to go further than ‘You experienced racism’; we have to understand their cultural perceptions,” she says. She suggests asking a question: “If you’re in Canada and everyone is equal, is what you experienced normal?” On this last point, Faty adds: “It’s up to us, the community workers on the front lines, to do this awareness-raising, to inform [newcomers] about their rights and responsibilities here in Quebec – rights and responsibilities that can be very different from those [that apply] in their countries of origin.”

Si tous les invités s’entendent sur la n: While all the guests agree on the need to teach newcomers their rights, some express reservations when it comes to encouraging them to turn to institutions and file complaints. Indeed, isn’t it asking too much of people who are already vulnerable to undertake such steps? To illustrate her point, Wideline shares the following two anecdotes with the rest of the group.
Un jour, son frère (un homme noir) et el: One day, she and her brother (a Black man) are walking on Lapierre Street in Montréal-Nord when a white homeless man approaches them and starts insulting them. “Dirty n****!” he shouts at Wideline’s brother. To her great surprise, her brother doesn’t flinch. He even laughs, then replies: “Me, that? You’re the one calling me a n****? I’m not that.” Wideline is even more surprised when the man backs down and apologizes to her brother. “That stayed with me,” she says.
The second anecdote comes from a friend. He, a Black man, is driving with an acquaintance, also a Black man. There is a lot of traffic on the road. At a stop, the driver of the next vehicle calls out to him, shouting “What’s your problem?”, in reference to a passing manoeuvre. Then he quickly calls him, once again, a “dirty n****.” Angry, Wideline’s friend immediately gets out of his car, followed by his friend. Tension rises, a fourth man – who is with the driver at the origin of the incident – gets out too, and a fight breaks out. “And since we live in modern times, people started filming… for the same N-word. Well, a complaint was filed against the two Black men. […] Even though the people in the other car were the ones who came to fight, who hit first, videos were brought in, and my friend had to do community service,” Wideline says.
Quelle leçon faut-il tirer de ces deux h: What lesson should be drawn from these two stories? According to Wideline, even when you experience an injustice, you need to step back for a moment, because “when you react without thinking, there are serious consequences.”
Elle poursuit : « Mon conseil, ce n’est: She continues: “My advice isn’t not to file a complaint, it’s to take a moment, think, and not bring problems on yourself. Because Black men, Black women with criminal records, that’s one more bullet in your foot as you try to get ahead in the system. So take a moment when you experience something. What you feel is legitimate, but take a moment and think further ahead. What do I do with what I felt: do I go further, do I file a complaint? Or do I talk with my friends, we clear our heads, I talk about it with a community worker… Think about your reaction. Because what comes after is just as important as the act. […] We’re not impulsive. We also know who we are, like my brother.”
Dans le groupe de discussion, les esprit: In the discussion group, tempers flare. What to do, for example, when you are refused housing for no valid reason?
Un autre participant suggère une solutio: Another participant suggests a way around having to turn to legal services openly: have CARI Saint-Laurent or other organizations ever thought of setting up a platform that would collect reports anonymously while indirectly raising awareness among anyone who commits racist acts? Currently, no such tool exists at CARI Saint-Laurent or elsewhere.
« Dans ces situations-là, si ça se passe: “In those situations, if it happens, I suggest talking to your integration counsellors first. We know of resources for reporting these incidents. There are housing assistance organizations if the person can’t react or act on their own […],” Faty replies. “If needed,” he adds, “organizations like CARI or housing committees can also mediate between tenants and landlords to find common ground.”
Wideline émet une réserve : « La réalité: Wideline voices a reservation: “The reality is that people have very few means. You experience racism, someone refuses to rent you an apartment because you’re Black, you go to the housing committee, which manages to take the appeal a bit further… these landlords will only pay small fines, which mean nothing to them. That’s the reality, and people need to know it. There’s a question to ask yourself: am I going to wear myself out finding a lawyer to sue someone who, in the end, will only have a small fine to pay? Or do I move on?”
Les propos de l’intervenante de l’ICI Mo: The ICI Montréal-Nord worker’s words draw nods of approval. She continues: “Very often, we’ll experience an act of racism and there will be no direct consequences for the person who committed it.”
Elle revient de nouveau sur la nécessité: She returns once again to the need to absorb the blow, to give yourself time to feel the whole range of emotions that can surface, regardless of what others say. “Then we can decide to act based on what we felt: ‘Am I going to seek justice? Am I going to undertake something, or, on the contrary, am I going to avoid this situation?’ ” she lists.
Loin de fermer la porte à la possibilité: Far from closing the door on the possibility of filing a complaint, she insists on the need to put yourself first throughout the process: “The most important thing is your mental, physical, financial, spiritual well-being – and there are battles, sometimes, that aren’t worth fighting. That’s not something they’ll tell you. They will always encourage you to file a complaint, but think of your well-being above all.”
Du côté des conseillers du CARI Saint-La: On the side of the CARI Saint-Laurent counsellors, a more integrated approach is put forward in responding to a racist act. At ICI Montréal-Nord, there is more promotion of a realistic approach. The first requires extra effort and a willingness to navigate the system once again, while the second focuses on the interplay of constraints in each person’s reality. Although there is tension between the two approaches, they are complementary up to a point. Trusting your own experience and doing what seems right for you, without needlessly compromising yourself, is a solution that seems to have convinced the community workers.
La conversation se conclut sur les mots: The conversation ends with Wideline’s words. “You’re the ones who get to decide, because it’s your fight. And it’s a fight that will last your whole life, unfortunately. If we’re here today, it’s because we’d like to put an end to this for our children. But one day at a time. For now, accept what you feel and don’t minimize it,” she concludes firmly.
